newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil 1996/97 cotton planting hits all-time low.
newsitem.headline: Brazil 1996/97 cotton planting hits all-time low.

text.p: Brazilian farmers are planting less cotton than ever and the 1996/97 crop is due to come in at just 309,400 tonnes, according to the Ministry of Agriculture's National Supply Company (Conab).
Planted area is forecast to drop to a historic low of 682,100 hectares as crop diseases and adverse weather pile on to farmers' financial woes, forcing them to turn to more profitable crops.
Even a recent rise in internal prices, fueled by low stocks and recent import financing restrictions, may not be enough to generate a turnaround in the beleaguered sector for 1997/98.
But not all economists believe Brazil will necessarily be the world's largest importer of cotton in 1997.

The latest crop estimate, the fourth produced by Conab this harvest, is down 12.8 percent from its previous forecast of a 355,100 tonne crop and down 24.5 percent from the 410,100 tonnes harvested in 1995/96.
"The adjustment in mainly due to a drop in production in the north-east," said Conab economist Asdrubal de Carvalho Jacobina.
"This was mainly due to the problem of crop diseases in Bahia state due to drought in January and afterwards, heavy rains which prevented the treatment of crop diseases," he added.
These caused a drop in both planted area and productivity and as a result, the crop in the north-east was set to drop to 73,500 tonnes from a previous estimate of 95,000 tonnes, Jacobina said.

Overall productivity was seen at 1,296 kilos of raw cotton per hectare, compared to initial expectations of 1,318 kilos. But this was up 5.4 percent on the 1,230 kilos per hectare registered last year, Jacobina said.
Conab forecasts Brazil will import 460,000 tonnes of cotton this year to satisfy internal demand.
This compares with imports of 385,300 tonnes in 1996, valued at $750 million.
"It could be that imports will be slightly higher. Some people are talking about 500,000 tonnes," Jacobino said. But Brazil is unlikely to be the world's largest importer this year, he added.
"We believe China will be the biggest importer this year with Brazil coming in third position," he said.
Agronomists believe the recent rise in internal prices could increase planting for the 1997/98 crop but say it is still too early to say by how much.
"Stocks are very low, equivalent to 15 days of consumption," said Jacobino. Prices have risen to around nine reais per 15-kg bale in the centre-south, compared to around 7.60 reais in January.
Economists say this could herald a turnaround for states like Parana, where planted area has dropped to its lowest level in history at 59,700 hectares, down 67 percent from 1995/96.
"There is some hope for a rise in planting next year, but we will have to wait until September to say," said Otmar Hubner, agronomist at the Parana agricultural secretariat.
With most cotton grown by small farmers whose production costs are high, it will probably take a more far-reaching government policy to produce any significant change, analysts said.
